content: Enhanced adherence counseling and additional viral load testing are essential to achieve and maintain viral load suppression in patients. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, same-day point-of-care viral load testing should be utilized whenever possible to expedite result availability and facilitate timely clinical decision-making. If same-day testing is not available, viral load specimens and results for these women should be prioritized throughout the laboratory referral process, including specimen collection, testing, and result return. Adherence counseling must be provided at all antenatal and postnatal visits to ensure sustained viral suppression during pregnancy and breastfeeding. For all pregnant women, regardless of when antiretroviral therapy (ART) was initiated, viral load testing should be conducted between 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at the latest, at delivery) to identify those at risk of treatment failure or perinatal transmission. If the viral load exceeds 1000 copies/mL, the treatment monitoring algorithm should be followed, and enhanced postnatal prophylaxis should be provided to the infant. For pregnant women who started ART before conception, a viral load test should be performed at the first antenatal care visit (or upon initial presentation) to identify those at increased risk of in utero transmission. If the viral load exceeds 1000 copies/mL, the treatment monitoring algorithm should be followed, and infant nucleic acid testing at birth should be considered where available. Regardless of maternal viral load, infants born to mothers who initiated ART at any time during pregnancy may be considered for birth testing where available. For all breastfeeding women, regardless of when ART was initiated, viral load testing should be conducted three months after delivery and every six months thereafter to detect viremic episodes during the postnatal period. Point-of-care viral load testing is recommended as a conditional approach to monitor treatment among people living with HIV on ART, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Since 2016, viral load testing has been the preferred method for monitoring HIV treatment, with significant uptake in lowand middle-income countries. However, challenges such as limited access, infrastructural barriers, human resource shortages, and long turnaround times persist. New point-of-care technologies have emerged, enabling simplified and rapid viral load testing with results available within 1–2 hours. These technologies, such as the Cepheid GeneXpert® and Abbott m-PIMA™, have undergone WHO prequalification and are being used in various settings. Point-of-care viral load testing has demonstrated shorter timeframes for result return and clinical action compared to standard laboratory-based testing. In randomized controlled trials, same-day results were available for clinicians and patients nearly 99% of the time with point-of-care testing, compared to significantly lower rates with standard testing. Long-term outcomes, such as viral load suppression and retention in care, were better among patients receiving point-of-care testing. For example, 90% of patients achieved viral suppression and retention in care after 12 months with point-of-care testing, compared to 76% with standard testing. Point-of-care viral load testing is cost-effective compared to laboratory-based testing, even when accounting for local contexts and implementation approaches. However, these studies did not include potential cost savings for patients, such as reduced facility visits. Surveys among people living with HIV and healthcare workers indicate a strong preference for point-of-care viral load testing due to its rapid results and ability to facilitate immediate treatment adjustments. However, concerns about increased workload for healthcare workers were noted. Ethical and equity considerations emphasize the importance of integrating point-of-care viral load testing into routine clinical care to promote social justice and equitable access to high-quality healthcare. Efforts should be made to address resource limitations and ensure the availability of necessary technologies to support this approach. Further research is needed to optimize treatment monitoring algorithms for pregnant and breastfeeding women on ART, as well as to understand the clinical relevance of low-level viremia and its relationship to drug resistance mutations.
